clue.text: Six hours every' three months

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a quarter of a twenty-four-hour day

definitions.note: describes when the answer falls rather than naming it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the legal days that open each quarter of the year, when rents fall due

explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe is a printing blemish. A quarter-day is one of the four days in the year, three months apart, when rents and contracts traditionally fell due in Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings take a fraction of a span: a quarter of one day's hours, and the dated term-day recurring each quarter of the year.

clue.text: As difficult as the search for water in nursery lore

parts.note: surface reading: a task as hard as a search

parts.words: the search for water in nursery lore
parts.note: setter's reading: Jack and Jill went up the hill to fetch a pail of water

explanation.surface: A task as hard as hunting for water in a children's rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: The nursery rhyme Jack and Jill sends the pair up a hill for water, which is where the climb comes from.
explanation.definitionFit: An uphill task is a laborious struggle, so the adjective means difficult.

clue.text: Root-stocks are right with homes that are about middle size

parts.note: R is the usual abbreviation for right

indicators.note: something that is about other letters goes around them

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: the middle of a word means only its central letters are kept

parts.note: the two central letters of the word size

explanation.surface: A gardener says root-stocks suit medium-sized houses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Middle size' reads as a phrase meaning medium, but 'middle' takes the heart of the word size.
explanation.definitionFit: A rhizome is a horizontal underground stem that sends out roots and shoots, which gardeners call a rootstock.

clue.text: Mince-pies policeman ate in church office

indicators.note: to mince is to chop up finely, so the word beside it is cut and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
a cop is a policeman
taken as written

explanation.surface: A constable eats mince pies at the parish office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mince-pies' looks like one Christmas treat, but the hyphen hides a verb working on the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: The episcopate is the position or term of office of a bishop, a rank within the church.

clue.text: Sirius shadows sailor

parts.note: to dog someone is to follow or shadow them
a tar is a sailor

explanation.surface: Someone named Sirius tails a seaman.
explanation.definitionFit: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky, lies in Canis Major and is popularly called by this canine name.

clue.text: Show sign of weariness, ' ascending the north route

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the letters are read from bottom to top

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for north
a way is a route

explanation.surface: A tired walker climbs the northern path.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe is a printing blemish.
explanation.definitionFit: Opening the mouth wide and breathing deeply is the body's reflex when tired or bored.

clue.text: Christian was one — true, mine is different

indicators.note: being different means changed, so the letters take a new order

parts.note: the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: A believer insists their faith differs from someone else's.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' looks like a believer; it is Fletcher Christian, who led the 1789 revolt on HMS Bounty.
explanation.definitionFit: Fletcher Christian seized HMS Bounty from Captain Bligh, so he was a sailor in open revolt against his officers.

clue.text: Headwear for a sleeper, you say? Sir, you've got it!

indicators.note: what you say is heard rather than read, so the sound counts and not the spelling

parts.note: a covering for the head worn at bedtime

explanation.surface: A shopper asks for a nightcap and the assistant hands it over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sir, you've got it' sounds like a shop assistant, but it is what a newly dubbed knight is told: the title Sir comes with the honour.
explanation.definitionFit: A knighthood is the honour that entitles a man to be addressed as Sir.

clue.text: Leaves time for Milton's Vallombrosa

parts.note: surface reading: someone allows time for a visit to an Italian valley
setter's reading: the season of falling leaves, as in Milton's simile of fallen leaves strewing the brooks of Vallombrosa

explanation.surface: A traveller sets aside time to visit the Tuscan valley Milton made famous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaves' looks like a verb but is the noun: the time of leaves. Paradise Lost compares fallen angels to leaves lying 'thick as autumnal leaves that strew the brooks in Vallombrosa'.
explanation.definitionFit: The season when trees shed their foliage is the time of fallen leaves, the very image Milton used for Vallombrosa.

clue.text: Doing well, getting six into the endless Wagnerian cycle

indicators.note: without an end, so the word it governs loses its final letter

parts.note: the word 'the' with its last letter cut

indicators.note: getting something into another word means placing it inside that word

parts.note: Wagner's four-opera cycle is known as the Ring
six in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: An opera company prospers by staging six performances of Wagner's Ring.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' sits beside the Wagner and seems to describe the famously long cycle, but it trims only the little word before it. Wagner's Der Ring des Nibelungen is a set of four operas.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrive is to prosper or flourish, so the present participle means doing well.

clue.text: A flat? Vocalist prefers the key of the prison

parts.words: A flat? Vocalist prefers the key of
parts.note: surface reading: a singer choosing a musical key such as A flat
setter's reading: the jail in New York State whose name is a doubled verb a vocalist would welcome

explanation.surface: A singer asks for A flat, preferring that key to any other.
explanation.walkthrough: The joke treats the prison's name as if it were a musical key a singer would naturally prefer, since a vocalist's job is to sing. The New York prison is at Ossining.
explanation.definitionFit: Sing Sing is the famous maximum-security penitentiary on the Hudson River in New York State.

clue.text: A century hit? -He keeps his trap shut

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
to lam is to thrash or strike

explanation.surface: A batsman scores a hundred, then keeps quiet about it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trap' is slang for mouth; the shellfish clamps its shell tight, which is why a silent person is said to clam up.
explanation.definitionFit: A bivalve shellfish keeps its shell closed, and the word also names a tight-lipped person who says nothing.

clue.text: English church about to war with Rome (some brain needed)

parts.note: CE is the Church of England
re means concerning, about
bellum is the Latin word for war
says the word is taken in the Romans' language

explanation.surface: The Church of England is about to go to war with the Vatican, which would take some thinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'With Rome' reads as fighting the Pope; it signals Latin, the language of Rome.
explanation.definitionFit: The cerebellum is the part of the brain at the back of the skull that coordinates movement.

clue.text: Work with beer. The aroma is colourful

parts.note: OP is short for opus, a musical work
ale is a kind of beer
a scent is an aroma

explanation.surface: A pub chat: working with beer, the smell becomes vivid.
explanation.definitionFit: Opalescent means showing shifting milky iridescent hues like an opal, so it is a fair synonym for colourful.

clue.text: Nothing extra nice? Confound and curse it!

indicators.note: to confound is to throw into confusion, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: nothing is zero, the shape of O
the two words supply the letters

explanation.surface: Someone finds nothing especially pleasant and swears in frustration.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Confound' and 'curse' look like a pair of oaths, but only the second half is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An execration is an uttered curse, and 'curse it!' is an example of such an outburst.

clue.text: Red being a risky sort of roulette gamble

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a Soviet communist, the Reds of the Cold War

definitions.text: a risky sort of roulette gamble
definitions.note: names the gamble; the answer is the word that qualifies it
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the deadly game with a revolver holding one bullet

explanation.surface: Betting on red at the wheel is a dangerous punt.
explanation.walkthrough: Red looks like the roulette bet, which is the trap; here it means a communist.
explanation.definitionFit: In Cold War usage a Red was a Soviet citizen, and Russian roulette is the lethal game of chance with a revolver.

clue.text: Main chemical characteristic

parts.note: surface reading: the principal property of a chemical
setter's reading: the main is the open sea, whose defining chemical feature is its salt

explanation.walkthrough: 'Main' looks like an adjective meaning chief; it is the old noun for the ocean, as in the Spanish Main.
explanation.definitionFit: Saltiness is the obvious chemical property of seawater, measured as the concentration of dissolved salts.

clue.text: Franck has one love, Viola

parts.note: the composer César Franck
I is the Roman numeral one
love is nil in tennis, the shape of O

explanation.surface: The composer Franck is devoted to the viola.
explanation.walkthrough: Viola looks like the instrument beloved of a composer; she is the heroine of Twelfth Night.
explanation.definitionFit: In Shakespeare's Twelfth Night the shipwrecked Viola disguises herself as a young man and takes the name Cesario.

clue.text: He's best in defence, they say

definitions.text: He's best in defence, they say

parts.note: surface reading: a player who excels as a defender
setter's reading: the proverb holds that attack is the best form of defence, so the best defender is one who goes forward

explanation.walkthrough: 'They say' is not a sound signal here; it marks a saying, the proverb that attack is the best form of defence.
explanation.definitionFit: If attacking is the best defence, the person who attacks is the best defender, which twists the proverb into a person.

clue.text: What Washington may have done to logic too?

definitions.text: What Washington may have done to logic too?

parts.note: surface reading: the boy George Washington cut down his father's cherry tree
setter's reading: logic-chopping is quibbling, so the same verb fits arguing over fine points

explanation.walkthrough: The legend has young George Washington confessing he could not tell a lie about felling the cherry tree; logic-chopping is pedantic hair-splitting.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb fits both cutting down a tree with an axe and the idiom for quibbling, logic-chopping.

clue.text: Ringleader appears somewhat sheepish

parts.note: surface reading: the chief of a gang of troublemakers
setter's reading: the leading ram of a flock, which wears a bell, is literally a sheep

explanation.surface: The gang's chief looks a little embarrassed when caught.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ringleader' splits as the one with the ringing bell who leads; 'sheepish' means embarrassed in the surface but here means sheep-like. A wether is a castrated ram.
explanation.definitionFit: The bell-wether is the belled ram that leads a flock, and the word is also used for anyone who leads others.

clue.text: Like the starting line of a Times letter?.

definitions.text: Like the starting line of a Times letter?

parts.words: the starting line of a Times letter
parts.note: surface reading: the opening of a letter to the editor of The Times
setter's reading: a starting line is the one runners toe, and loyal correspondents toe the line

explanation.surface: Someone describes the formal opening of a letter to The Times.
explanation.walkthrough: To toe the line is to set the feet at the start of a race, and figuratively to conform; a dutiful letter-writer's first line conforms to the paper's form. This parse is tentative.
explanation.definitionFit: A starting line is one that runners place their feet against, so it is a line that is toed.

clue.text: Worn out, using two keys to open a village function

parts.note: E and F are musical keys
a fete is a village fair, a British summer fundraising event with stalls and games

explanation.surface: An exhausted organist uses two keys to start the village fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'To open' puts the keys at the front of the event, the way a dignitary opens a fete.
explanation.definitionFit: Effete means exhausted of vigour, no longer productive, hence worn out.

clue.text: Boomer qualified for this Games event, thanks to Dingo

definitions.text: Boomer qualified for this Games event, thanks to Dingo

parts.words: Boomer qualified for this Games event
parts.note: surface reading: an athlete nicknamed Boomer earns a place at the Games
setter's reading: a kangaroo, chased by a wild dog, has had plenty of practice at covering ground in great bounds

explanation.surface: An Australian athlete got into a Games event with a teammate's help.
explanation.walkthrough: A boomer is a large male kangaroo, and the dingo is Australia's wild dog; fleeing one would make any kangaroo a field-event specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: The athletics event for distance leaping suits an animal that escapes predators by bounding far.

clue.text: Ruin a French party

parts.note: un is French for a
a do is a party

explanation.surface: Someone wrecks a celebration held in France.
explanation.definitionFit: To undo someone is to bring about their downfall, so the verb is a synonym of ruin.

clue.text: Points to effect of tropical heat on the skin

definitions.meaning: first meaning: sharp spines or thorns

definitions.text: effect of tropical heat on the skin
definitions.meaning: second meaning: a stinging, tingling sensation, as in prickly heat

explanation.surface: Someone indicates what hot climates do to one's complexion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Points to' reads as indicates, but the definition stops at 'Points' and 'to' only joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Prickles are thorns or spines, and the word also names the tingling rash called prickly heat in hot climates.

clue.text: What Sheffield would be if it turned loose

indicators.note: turned here means twisted around, so the club's word is reworked

parts.note: Sheffield United is the city's football club

explanation.surface: A football fan wonders what would happen if Sheffield's team went wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Sheffield United is an English football club; its second name is the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Something untied is unfastened, free of its knots, and so it is loose.

clue.text: Usual heraldic charges

parts.note: surface reading: the fees normally made by the College of Arms
setter's reading: in heraldry a charge is a device on a shield, and the simplest are named for being usual

explanation.surface: The standard fees a herald asks for designing a coat of arms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' suggests payments, but in heraldry a charge is a figure borne on the shield; 'Usual' hints at the adjective hidden in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry the ordinaries are the simplest geometric figures on a shield, such as the bend, chevron and pale.
